Chapter 10 - Trigonometric Identi.question_text: The diagram shows an isosceles right-angled triangle $ABC$. $AE = DE = 1$ unit and $\angle ACD = 30^\circ$. a (i) Calculate the exact length of $CE$.
Chapter 10 - Trigonometric Identi.hint: Use $\triangle ADE$ to find $AD$, then use the sine rule in $\triangle ADC$ to find $AC$ and hence $CE=AC-AE$.
Chapter 10 - Trigonometric Identi.correct_answer: $AE=DE=1,\ \triangle ADE\text{ is right-angled isosceles at }E\Rightarrow AD^2=1^2+1^2=2\Rightarrow AD=\sqrt2;\ \text{in }\triangle ADC,\ AD/\sin30^\circ = AC/\sin105^\circ\Rightarrow AC=AD\cdot\dfrac{\sin105^\circ}{\sin30^\circ}=\sqrt2\cdot\dfrac{\sin(60^\circ+45^\circ)}{1/2}=\sqrt2\cdot\dfrac{\frac{\sqrt6+\sqrt2}{4}}{1/2}=\sqrt2\cdot\dfrac{\sqrt6+\sqrt2}{2}=\sqrt3+1;\ CE=AC-AE=(\sqrt3+1)-1=\sqrt3.$

Chapter 10 - Trigonometric Identi.question_text: The diagram shows an isosceles right-angled triangle $ABC$. $AE = DE = 1$ unit and $\angle ACD = 30^\circ$. a (ii) Calculate the exact length of $DC$.

Chapter 10 - Trigonometric Identi.question_text: The diagram shows an isosceles right-angled triangle $ABC$. $AE = DE = 1$ unit and $\angle ACD = 30^\circ$. c (i) Hence find the exact value of $\sin15^\circ$.

Chapter 10 - Trigonometric Identi.hint: Interpret $\tan B=\dfrac{\text{opp}}{\text{adj}}=\dfrac{\sqrt{21}}{2}$, find the hypotenuse, then use quadrant III where $\sin B<0$.
Chapter 10 - Trigonometric Identi.correct_answer: Take opposite side $\sqrt{21}$ and adjacent side $2$ so $\text{hyp}=\sqrt{(\sqrt{21})^2+2^2}=\sqrt{21+4}=5$; hence $\sin B=\dfrac{\sqrt{21}}{5}$ in magnitude but $B$ is obtuse with $\tan B>0$ so $B$ lies in quadrant III and $\sin B<0$, giving $\sin B=-\dfrac{\sqrt{21}}{5}.$

Chapter 10 - Trigonometric Identi.question_text: Given that angle $B$ is obtuse and $\tan B=\dfrac{\sqrt{21}}{2}$, find the exact value of: b $\cos B$.
Chapter 10 - Trigonometric Identi.hint: Use the same triangle as in part (a) and sign of cosine in quadrant III.
Chapter 10 - Trigonometric Identi.correct_answer: With adjacent $2$ and hypotenuse $5$, $\cos B=\dfrac{2}{5}$ in magnitude but $B$ is in quadrant III where $\cos B<0$, so $\cos B=-\dfrac25.$

Chapter 10 - Trigonometric Identi.question_text: Simplify the expression: a $\cos^4\theta-\sin^4\theta$.
Chapter 10 - Trigonometric Identi.hint: Recognise a difference of squares and use $\sin^2\theta+\cos^2\theta=1$.

Chapter 10 - Trigonometric Identi.question_text: Simplify the expression: b $\sin^23\theta-\sin^23\theta\cos^23\theta$.
Simplify the expression: c $\cos^4\theta+2\sin^2\theta\cos^2\theta+\sin^4\theta$.
Chapter 10 - Trigonometric Identi.hint: Recognise a perfect square and use $\sin^2\theta+\cos^2\theta=1$.

Chapter 10 - Trigonometric Identi.question_title: Find $\tan x$ from linear trig eqn
Chapter 10 - Trigonometric Identi.question_text: Given that $2(\sin x+2\cos x)=\sin x+5\cos x$, find the exact value of $\tan x$.
Chapter 10 - Trigonometric Identi.hint: Expand, collect like terms, then divide by $\cos x$.
Chapter 10 - Trigonometric Identi.correct_answer: $2(\sin x+2\cos x)=\sin x+5\cos x\Rightarrow2\sin x+4\cos x=\sin x+5\cos x\Rightarrow\sin x-\cos x=0\Rightarrow\sin x=\cos x\Rightarrow\tan x=\dfrac{\sin x}{\cos x}=1.$

Chapter 10 - Trigonometric Identi.question_title: Express $\tan y$ in terms of $\tan x$
Chapter 10 - Trigonometric Identi.question_text: Given that $\sin x\cos y+3\cos x\sin y=2\sin x\sin y-4\cos x\cos y$, express $\tan y$ in terms of $\tan x$.
Chapter 10 - Trigonometric Identi.hint: Divide the equation by $\cos x\cos y$ and solve the resulting linear equation in $\tan y$.
Chapter 10 - Trigonometric Identi.correct_answer: $\dfrac{\sin x\cos y}{\cos x\cos y}+3\dfrac{\cos x\sin y}{\cos x\cos y}=2\dfrac{\sin x\sin y}{\cos x\cos y}-4\dfrac{\cos x\cos y}{\cos x\cos y}\Rightarrow\tan x+3\tan y=2\tan x\tan y-4;$ letting $\tan x=t,\ \tan y=u$ gives $t+3u=2tu-4\Rightarrow3u-2tu=-4-t\Rightarrow u(3-2t)=-(4+t)\Rightarrow u=\dfrac{t+4}{2t-3};$ hence $\tan y=\dfrac{\tan x+4}{2\tan x-3}.$

Chapter 10 - Trigonometric Identi.question_text: Prove that, for all values of $\theta$: a $(1+\sin\theta)^2+\cos^2\theta\equiv2(1+\sin\theta)$.
Prove that, for all values of $\theta$: b $\cos^4\theta+\sin^2\theta\equiv\sin^4\theta+\cos^2\theta$.
Chapter 10 - Trigonometric Identi.hint: Start from the difference LHS$-$RHS, factor, and use $\sin^2\theta+\cos^2\theta=1$.

Chapter 10 - Trigonometric Identi.question_text: Without attempting to solve them, state how many solutions the equation $2\sin\theta=3$ has in the interval $0^\circ\le\theta\le360^\circ$.
Chapter 10 - Trigonometric Identi.hint: Give the range of $\sin\theta$ and compare with the required value.
Chapter 10 - Trigonometric Identi.correct_answer: $2\sin\theta=3\Rightarrow\sin\theta=1.5$, but $-1\le\sin\theta\le1$ for all real $\theta$, so $\sin\theta=1.5$ is impossible and there are $\boxed{0\text{ solutions}}$.

Chapter 10 - Trigonometric Identi.question_text: Without attempting to solve them, state how many solutions the equation $\sin\theta=-\cos\theta$ has in the interval $0^\circ\le\theta\le360^\circ$.
Chapter 10 - Trigonometric Identi.hint: Rewrite as $\tan\theta$ and use its period and signs.
Chapter 10 - Trigonometric Identi.correct_answer: $\sin\theta=-\cos\theta\Rightarrow\tan\theta=-1$. The reference angle is $45^\circ$ and $\tan\theta<0$ in quadrants II and IV, so $\theta=135^\circ,315^\circ$. Hence there are $\boxed{2\text{ solutions}}$.

Chapter 10 - Trigonometric Identi.question_text: Without attempting to solve them, state how many solutions the equation $2\sin\theta+3\cos\theta+6=0$ has in the interval $0^\circ\le\theta\le360^\circ$.
Chapter 10 - Trigonometric Identi.hint: Use the maximum possible value of $2\sin\theta+3\cos\theta$ as $R\sin(\theta+\alpha)$ with $R=\sqrt{2^2+3^2}$.
Chapter 10 - Trigonometric Identi.correct_answer: The expression $2\sin\theta+3\cos\theta$ has range $[-\sqrt{13},\sqrt{13}]$ with $\sqrt{13}\approx3.6$, so $2\sin\theta+3\cos\theta+6\ge-3.6+6>0$ for all $\theta$, hence it can never be $0$ and there are $\boxed{0\text{ solutions}}$.

Chapter 10 - Trigonometric Identi.question_text: Without attempting to solve them, state how many solutions the equation $\tan\theta+\dfrac1{\tan\theta}=0$ has in the interval $0^\circ\le\theta\le360^\circ$.
Chapter 10 - Trigonometric Identi.hint: Multiply both sides by $\tan\theta$ (excluding $\tan\theta=0$) and inspect the resulting quadratic.
Chapter 10 - Trigonometric Identi.correct_answer: $\tan\theta+\dfrac1{\tan\theta}=0\Rightarrow\tan^2\theta+1=0$, but $\tan^2\theta+1>0$ for all real $\theta$, so the equation has $\boxed{0\text{ solutions}}$.

Chapter 10 - Trigonometric Identi.question_text: Factorise $4xy-y^2+4x-y$.
Chapter 10 - Trigonometric Identi.hint: Group terms and factorise by grouping.

Chapter 10 - Trigonometric Identi.question_text: Solve the equation $4\sin\theta\cos\theta-\cos^2\theta+4\sin\theta-\cos\theta=0$ in the interval $0^\circ\le\theta\le360^\circ$.
Chapter 10 - Trigonometric Identi.hint: Factorise by grouping to get a product of two factors then solve each.
Chapter 10 - Trigonometric Identi.correct_answer: $4\sin\theta\cos\theta-\cos^2\theta+4\sin\theta-\cos\theta=4\sin\theta(\cos\theta+1)-\cos\theta(\cos\theta+1)=(\cos\theta+1)(4\sin\theta-\cos\theta)=0$. So $\cos\theta+1=0$ or $4\sin\theta-\cos\theta=0$. First gives $\cos\theta=-1\Rightarrow\theta=180^\circ$. Second gives $4\sin\theta=\cos\theta\Rightarrow\tan\theta=\tfrac14$ with reference angle $\tan^{-1}(\tfrac14)\approx14.0^\circ$, so $\theta\approx14.0^\circ,194.0^\circ$. Thus $\theta\approx14.0^\circ,180^\circ,194.0^\circ$.

Chapter 10 - Trigonometric Identi.question_text: Express $4\cos3\theta-\sin(90^\circ-3\theta)$ as a single trigonometric function.
Hence solve $4\cos3\theta-\sin(90^\circ-3\theta)=2$ in the interval $0^\circ\le\theta\le360^\circ$, giving answers to $3$ significant figures.
Chapter 10 - Trigonometric Identi.hint: Use part (a) to write the equation as $3\cos3\theta=2$, then solve $\cos3\theta=\tfrac23$ for $3\theta$ between $0^\circ$ and $1080^\circ$.
Chapter 10 - Trigonometric Identi.correct_answer: From (a), $3\cos3\theta=2\Rightarrow\cos3\theta=\tfrac23$. Let $\alpha=\cos^{-1}(\tfrac23)\approx48.2^\circ$. Then $3\theta=\alpha,360^\circ-\alpha,360^\circ+\alpha,720^\circ-\alpha,720^\circ+\alpha,1080^\circ-\alpha\approx48.2^\circ,311.8^\circ,408.2^\circ,671.8^\circ,768.2^\circ,1031.8^\circ$. Dividing by $3$ gives $\theta\approx16.1^\circ,103.9^\circ,136.1^\circ,223.9^\circ,256.1^\circ,343.9^\circ$ (all to $3$ s.f.).

Chapter 10 - Trigonometric Identi.question_text: Given that $2\sin2\theta=\cos2\theta$, show that $\tan2\theta=0.5$.
Hence find the values of $\theta$, to one decimal place, in the interval $0^\circ\le\theta\le360^\circ$ for which $2\sin2\theta=\cos2\theta$.
Chapter 10 - Trigonometric Identi.hint: Use $\tan2\theta=0.5$ so $2\theta$ lies in quadrants I and III between $0^\circ$ and $720^\circ$.
Chapter 10 - Trigonometric Identi.correct_answer: From (a) $\tan2\theta=0.5$. Reference angle is $\alpha=\tan^{-1}(0.5)\approx26.6^\circ$. For $0^\circ\le2\theta\le720^\circ$, $2\theta=\alpha,180^\circ+\alpha,360^\circ+\alpha,540^\circ+\alpha\approx26.6^\circ,206.6^\circ,386.6^\circ,566.6^\circ$. Hence $\theta\approx13.3^\circ,103.3^\circ,193.3^\circ,283.3^\circ$ (to $1$ d.p.).

Chapter 10 - Trigonometric Identi.question_text: Find all the values of $\theta$ in the interval $0^\circ\le\theta\le360^\circ$ for which $\cos(\theta+75^\circ)=0.5$.
Chapter 10 - Trigonometric Identi.hint: Set $\phi=\theta+75^\circ$, solve $\cos\phi=0.5$, then subtract $75^\circ$ and adjust into $[0^\circ,360^\circ]$.
Chapter 10 - Trigonometric Identi.correct_answer: $\cos(\theta+75^\circ)=0.5\Rightarrow\cos\phi=0.5$ with $\phi=\theta+75^\circ$. Thus $\phi=60^\circ,300^\circ$ (mod $360^\circ$). Hence $\theta=-15^\circ,225^\circ$; adding $360^\circ$ to the negative value gives $\theta=225^\circ,345^\circ$. Therefore $\theta=225^\circ,345^\circ$.

Chapter 10 - Trigonometric Identi.question_text: Find all the values of $\theta$ in the interval $0^\circ\le\theta\le360^\circ$ for which $\sin2\theta=0.7$, giving answers to one decimal place.
Chapter 10 - Trigonometric Identi.hint: Solve for $2\theta$ in $[0^\circ,720^\circ]$ using $\alpha=\sin^{-1}(0.7)$ and the sine symmetry.

Chapter 10 - Trigonometric Identi.question_text: Find the values of $x$ in the interval $0^\circ\le x\le270^\circ$ which satisfy $\dfrac{\cos2x+0.5}{1-\cos2x}=2$.
Chapter 10 - Trigonometric Identi.hint: Set $c=\cos2x$, solve the linear equation in $c$, then solve $\cos2x=\tfrac12$ in $[0^\circ,540^\circ]$.

Chapter 10 - Trigonometric Identi.question_text: Find, in degrees, the values of $\theta$ in the interval $0^\circ\le\theta\le360^\circ$ for which $2\cos^2\theta-\cos\theta-1=\sin^2\theta$, giving answers to $1$ decimal place where appropriate.
Chapter 10 - Trigonometric Identi.hint: Use $\sin^2\theta=1-\cos^2\theta$ to form a quadratic in $\cos\theta$, solve, then convert to angles.
Chapter 10 - Trigonometric Identi.correct_answer: Let $c=\cos\theta$. Then $2c^2-c-1=1-c^2\Rightarrow3c^2-c-2=0\Rightarrow(3c+2)(c-1)=0$, so $c=1$ or $c=-\tfrac23$. Thus $\cos\theta=1\Rightarrow\theta=0^\circ,360^\circ$, and $\cos\theta=-\tfrac23\Rightarrow\theta\approx131.8^\circ,228.2^\circ$. Hence $\theta\approx0^\circ,131.8^\circ,228.2^\circ,360^\circ$.

Chapter 10 - Trigonometric Identi.question_text: A teacher asks a student to solve $2\sin3x=1$ for $-360^\circ\le x\le360^\circ$; the student writes $\sin3x=\tfrac12,\ 3x=30^\circ,\ x=10^\circ,\ \text{additional solution at }180^\circ-10^\circ=170^\circ$. Identify two mistakes.
Chapter 10 - Trigonometric Identi.hint: Compare the correct sine-solving procedure with what the student did.
Chapter 10 - Trigonometric Identi.correct_answer: First, the student found only one value $3x=30^\circ$ instead of all values of $3x$ with $\sin3x=\tfrac12$ in the interval $-1080^\circ\le3x\le1080^\circ$. Second, the symmetry $180^\circ-\alpha$ must be applied to $3x$, not to $x$, so subtracting $10^\circ$ from $180^\circ$ to get another $x$ is incorrect and also misses many further solutions.

Chapter 10 - Trigonometric Identi.question_text: Solve the equation $2\sin3x=1$ in the interval $-360^\circ\le x\le360^\circ$.
Chapter 10 - Trigonometric Identi.hint: Set $y=3x$, solve $\sin y=\tfrac12$ for $-1080^\circ\le y\le1080^\circ$, then divide by $3$.
Chapter 10 - Trigonometric Identi.correct_answer: $2\sin3x=1\Rightarrow\sin3x=\tfrac12$. Let $y=3x$. Then $\sin y=\tfrac12$ so $y=30^\circ+360^\circ k$ or $y=150^\circ+360^\circ k$. For $-1080^\circ\le y\le1080^\circ$ this gives $y=-1050^\circ,-690^\circ,-330^\circ,30^\circ,390^\circ,750^\circ,-930^\circ,-570^\circ,-210^\circ,150^\circ,510^\circ,870^\circ$. Dividing by $3$ yields $x=-350^\circ,-230^\circ,-110^\circ,10^\circ,130^\circ,250^\circ,-310^\circ,-190^\circ,-70^\circ,50^\circ,170^\circ,290^\circ$. Restricting to $-360^\circ\le x\le360^\circ$, the solutions are $x=-350^\circ,-310^\circ,-230^\circ,-190^\circ,-110^\circ,-70^\circ,10^\circ,50^\circ,130^\circ,170^\circ,250^\circ,290^\circ$.

Chapter 10 - Trigonometric Identi.question_text: Sketch the graphs of $y=3\sin x$ and $y=2\cos x$ on the same set of axes ($0^\circ\le x\le360^\circ$).
Chapter 10 - Trigonometric Identi.hint: Mark key points using amplitudes $3$ and $2$ and the usual $90^\circ$ step for sine and cosine.
Chapter 10 - Trigonometric Identi.correct_answer: $y=3\sin x$ is a sine wave with amplitude $3$ passing through $(0,0)$, $(90^\circ,3)$, $(180^\circ,0)$, $(270^\circ,-3)$, $(360^\circ,0)$. The graph $y=2\cos x$ has amplitude $2$ and passes through $(0^\circ,2)$, $(90^\circ,0)$, $(180^\circ,-2)$, $(270^\circ,0)$, $(360^\circ,2)$. Plot these key points and draw smooth periodic curves.

Chapter 10 - Trigonometric Identi.question_text: From the graphs, write down how many solutions there are in the given range for the equation $3\sin x=2\cos x$.
Chapter 10 - Trigonometric Identi.hint: Observe how many intersection points the two curves have between $0^\circ$ and $360^\circ$.
Chapter 10 - Trigonometric Identi.correct_answer: The graphs $y=3\sin x$ and $y=2\cos x$ intersect twice in $0^\circ\le x\le360^\circ$, once in quadrant I and once in quadrant III, so there are $\boxed{2}$ solutions.

Chapter 10 - Trigonometric Identi.question_text: Solve the equation $3\sin x=2\cos x$ algebraically, giving your answers in $0^\circ\le x\le360^\circ$ to one decimal place.
Chapter 10 - Trigonometric Identi.hint: Divide both sides by $\cos x$ to form a tangent equation and then use the CAST diagram.
Chapter 10 - Trigonometric Identi.correct_answer: $3\sin x=2\cos x\Rightarrow\tan x=\dfrac{2}{3}$. The reference angle is $\alpha=\tan^{-1}\left(\tfrac23\right)\approx33.7^\circ$. Since $\tan x>0$, $x$ lies in quadrants I and III: $x\approx33.7^\circ$ or $x\approx180^\circ+33.7^\circ=213.7^\circ$. Thus $x\approx33.7^\circ,213.7^\circ$ (to $1$ d.p.).

Chapter 10 - Trigonometric Identi.question_text: The diagram shows triangle $ABC$ with $AB=11\text{ cm}$, $BC=6\text{ cm}$ and $AC=7\text{ cm}$. a Find the exact value of $\cos B$, giving your answer in simplest form.
Chapter 10 - Trigonometric Identi.hint: Use the cosine rule with side $AC$ opposite angle $B$.
Chapter 10 - Trigonometric Identi.correct_answer: By the cosine rule, $AC^2=AB^2+BC^2-2(AB)(BC)\cos B\Rightarrow7^2=11^2+6^2-2\cdot11\cdot6\cos B\Rightarrow49=121+36-132\cos B\Rightarrow132\cos B=108\Rightarrow\cos B=\dfrac{108}{132}=\dfrac{9}{11}$.

Chapter 10 - Trigonometric Identi.question_text: Hence find the exact value of $\sin B$.
Chapter 10 - Trigonometric Identi.hint: Use $\sin^2B=1-\cos^2B$ and that $B$ is acute so $\sin B>0$.

Chapter 10 - Trigonometric Identi.question_text: The diagram shows triangle $PQR$ with $PR=6\text{ cm}$, $QR=5\text{ cm}$ and angle $QPR=45^\circ$. a Show that $\sin Q=\dfrac{3\sqrt2}{5}$.
Chapter 10 - Trigonometric Identi.hint: Apply the sine rule with sides $PR$ and $QR$ opposite angles $Q$ and $P$.
Chapter 10 - Trigonometric Identi.correct_answer: By the sine rule, $\dfrac{PR}{\sin Q}=\dfrac{QR}{\sin P}\Rightarrow\dfrac{6}{\sin Q}=\dfrac{5}{\sin45^\circ}=\dfrac{5}{\tfrac{\sqrt2}{2}}=\dfrac{10}{\sqrt2}$. Hence $\sin Q=\dfrac{6\sqrt2}{10}=\dfrac{3\sqrt2}{5}$.

Chapter 10 - Trigonometric Identi.question_text: Given that $Q$ is obtuse, find the exact value of $\cos Q$.
Chapter 10 - Trigonometric Identi.hint: Use $\cos^2Q=1-\sin^2Q$ and choose the negative square root because $Q$ is obtuse.
Chapter 10 - Trigonometric Identi.correct_answer: $\sin Q=\dfrac{3\sqrt2}{5}\Rightarrow\sin^2Q=\dfrac{18}{25}\Rightarrow\cos^2Q=1-\dfrac{18}{25}=\dfrac{7}{25}\Rightarrow\cos Q=-\dfrac{\sqrt7}{5}$ since $Q$ is obtuse and $\cos Q<0$.

Chapter 10 - Trigonometric Identi.question_text: Show that the equation $3\sin^2x-\cos^2x=2$ can be written as $4\sin^2x=3$.
Hence solve the equation $3\sin^2x-\cos^2x=2$ in the interval $-180^\circ\le x\le180^\circ$, giving your answers to one decimal place.
Chapter 10 - Trigonometric Identi.hint: Use $4\sin^2x=3$ to find $\sin x=\pm\dfrac{\sqrt3}{2}$ and then list all such angles in the interval.
Chapter 10 - Trigonometric Identi.correct_answer: From (a) $4\sin^2x=3\Rightarrow\sin^2x=\dfrac34\Rightarrow\sin x=\pm\dfrac{\sqrt3}{2}$. Thus $x=\pm60^\circ,\pm120^\circ$ in $[-180^\circ,180^\circ]$. To one decimal place, $x\approx-120.0^\circ,-60.0^\circ,60.0^\circ,120.0^\circ$.

Chapter 10 - Trigonometric Identi.question_text: Find all the solutions to the equation $3\cos^2x+1=4\sin x$ in the interval $-360^\circ\le x\le360^\circ$, giving your answers to $1$ decimal place.
Chapter 10 - Trigonometric Identi.hint: Rewrite $\cos^2x$ as $1-\sin^2x$, form a quadratic in $\sin x$, solve, then use the sine symmetry to list all angles in the interval.
Chapter 10 - Trigonometric Identi.correct_answer: $3\cos^2x+1=4\sin x\Rightarrow3(1-\sin^2x)+1=4\sin x\Rightarrow4-3\sin^2x=4\sin x\Rightarrow3\sin^2x+4\sin x-4=0$. Let $s=\sin x$. Then $3s^2+4s-4=0\Rightarrow s=\dfrac{-4\pm\sqrt{16+48}}{6}=\dfrac{-4\pm8}{6}$, so $s=\dfrac23$ or $s=-2$ (rejected). Thus $\sin x=\dfrac23$. Reference angle $\alpha=\sin^{-1}\!\left(\tfrac23\right)\approx41.8^\circ$. General solutions are $x=\alpha+360k^\circ$ or $x=180^\circ-\alpha+360k^\circ$. For $-360^\circ\le x\le360^\circ$ this gives $x\approx41.8^\circ,138.2^\circ,-318.2^\circ,-221.8^\circ$. So $x\approx-318.2^\circ,-221.8^\circ,41.8^\circ,138.2^\circ$ (to $1$ d.p.).

Chapter 10 - Trigonometric Identi.question_text: Solve the equation $\tan^2x-3\tan x+2=0$ in the interval $0^\circ\le x\le360^\circ$.
Chapter 10 - Trigonometric Identi.hint: Factor the quadratic in $\tan x$ and then solve $\tan x=1$ and $\tan x=2$ using the $180^\circ$ period.
Chapter 10 - Trigonometric Identi.correct_answer: $\tan^2x-3\tan x+2=0\Rightarrow(\tan x-1)(\tan x-2)=0\Rightarrow\tan x=1\text{ or }\tan x=2$. For $\tan x=1$, $x=45^\circ,225^\circ$. For $\tan x=2$, reference angle $\beta=\tan^{-1}2\approx63.4^\circ$, so $x\approx63.4^\circ,243.4^\circ$. Hence $x\approx45.0^\circ,63.4^\circ,225.0^\circ,243.4^\circ$ (to $1$ d.p.).

Chapter 10 - Trigonometric Identi.question_text: $$\text{The graph shows }y=\sin(x+45^\circ)\text{ for }-360^\circ\le x\le 360^\circ.\ \text{Write down the coordinates of each point where the curve crosses the x-axis.}$$
Chapter 10 - Trigonometric Identi.hint: $$\text{Set }y=0:\ \sin(x+45^\circ)=0\Rightarrow x+45^\circ=180^\circ n,\ n\in\mathbb{Z}.\ \text{List all }x\text{ in the given interval.}$$
Chapter 10 - Trigonometric Identi.correct_answer: $$\begin{aligned}\sin(x+45^\circ)=0&\Rightarrow x+45^\circ=180^\circ n\\x&=180^\circ n-45^\circ\\\text{Now choose integers }n\text{ so that }-360^\circ\le x\le360^\circ:\\n=-1&\Rightarrow x=-225^\circ\\n=0&\Rightarrow x=-45^\circ\\n=1&\Rightarrow x=135^\circ\\n=2&\Rightarrow x=315^\circ\\n=3&\Rightarrow x=495^\circ\ (\text{too large}),\ n=-2\Rightarrow x=-405^\circ\ (\text{too small})\\\Rightarrow\ \text{x-axis crossings: }&(-225^\circ,0),\ (-45^\circ,0),\ (135^\circ,0),\ (315^\circ,0)\end{aligned}$$

Chapter 10 - Trigonometric Identi.question_text: $$\text{The graph shows }y=\sin(x+45^\circ)\text{ for }-360^\circ\le x\le 360^\circ.\ \text{Write down the coordinates of the point where the curve crosses the y-axis.}$$
$$\text{A pyramid has four triangular faces and a square base. All the edges of the pyramid are the same length }s\text{ cm. Show that the total surface area is }(\sqrt3+1)s^2\text{ cm}^2.$$
Chapter 10 - Trigonometric Identi.hint: $$\text{If all edges are }s,\ \text{each triangular face has three sides }s\Rightarrow\text{equilateral. Find area of 4 faces + base.}$$
Chapter 10 - Trigonometric Identi.correct_answer: $$\begin{aligned}\text{Base: }&\text{square of side }s\Rightarrow A_{\text{base}}=s^2\\\text{Each triangular face: }&\text{two slant edges }=s\text{ and base edge }=s\\&\Rightarrow \text{each face is an equilateral triangle of side }s\\\text{Area of one equilateral triangle: }&A_{\triangle}=\frac{\sqrt3}{4}s^2\\\text{Four faces: }&A_{\text{faces}}=4\cdot\frac{\sqrt3}{4}s^2=\sqrt3\,s^2\\\text{Total surface area: }&A_{\text{total}}=A_{\text{base}}+A_{\text{faces}}=s^2+\sqrt3\,s^2=(\sqrt3+1)s^2\ \text{cm}^2\end{aligned}$$

Chapter 10 - Trigonometric Identi.question_text: $$\text{Find all solutions in }0^\circ\le x<360^\circ\text{ of }2\tan^2x-4=5\tan x,\ \text{giving each solution to 1 d.p.}$$
Chapter 10 - Trigonometric Identi.hint: $$\text{Let }t=\tan x.\ \text{Solve the quadratic }2t^2-5t-4=0,\ \text{then convert each }t\text{ to angles in }[0^\circ,360^\circ).$$
Chapter 10 - Trigonometric Identi.correct_answer: $$\begin{aligned}2\tan^2x-4&=5\tan x\\\text{Let }t=\tan x\Rightarrow 2t^2-5t-4&=0\\t&=\frac{5\pm\sqrt{25+32}}{4}=\frac{5\pm\sqrt{57}}{4}\\\sqrt{57}&\approx7.5498\\t_1&=\frac{5+7.5498}{4}\approx3.1375,\quad t_2=\frac{5-7.5498}{4}\approx-0.6375\\\text{Now find angles: }&x=\arctan(t)+180^\circ k\\\arctan(3.1375)&\approx72.2^\circ\Rightarrow x\approx72.2^\circ,\ 252.2^\circ\\\arctan(-0.6375)&\approx-32.5^\circ\Rightarrow x\approx147.5^\circ,\ 327.5^\circ\\\Rightarrow\ \text{Solutions: }&x\approx72.2^\circ,\ 147.5^\circ,\ 252.2^\circ,\ 327.5^\circ\end{aligned}$$

Chapter 10 - Trigonometric Identi.question_text: $$\text{Find all solutions in }0^\circ\le x<360^\circ\text{ of }5\sin^2x=6(1-\cos x),\ \text{giving each solution to 1 d.p.}$$
Chapter 10 - Trigonometric Identi.hint: $$\text{Use }\sin^2x=1-\cos^2x.\ \text{Let }c=\cos x\text{ to get a quadratic, then convert back to angles.}$$
Chapter 10 - Trigonometric Identi.correct_answer: $$\begin{aligned}5\sin^2x&=6(1-\cos x)\\5(1-\cos^2x)&=6-6\cos x\\5-5\cos^2x&=6-6\cos x\\0&=1-6\cos x+5\cos^2x\\5c^2-6c+1&=0\quad(c=\cos x)\\c&=\frac{6\pm\sqrt{36-20}}{10}=\frac{6\pm4}{10}\\\Rightarrow c&=1\ \text{or}\ c=0.2\\\cos x=1&\Rightarrow x=0^\circ\ (\text{and }360^\circ\text{ excluded})\\\cos x=0.2&\Rightarrow x=\arccos(0.2)\approx78.5^\circ\ \text{or}\ 360^\circ-78.5^\circ\approx281.5^\circ\\\Rightarrow\ \text{Solutions: }&x\approx0.0^\circ,\ 78.5^\circ,\ 281.5^\circ\end{aligned}$$

Chapter 10 - Trigonometric Identi.question_text: $$\text{Prove that }\cos^2x(\tan^2x+1)=1\text{ for all }x\text{ where }\cos x\text{ and }\tan x\text{ are defined.}$$
Chapter 10 - Trigonometric Identi.hint: $$\text{Use }\tan x=\frac{\sin x}{\cos x}\text{ and }\sin^2x+\cos^2x=1.\ \text{Simplify step by step.}$$

$$\text{Find all solutions in }0^\circ\le x\le360^\circ\text{ to }8\sin^2x+6\cos x-9=0,\ \text{giving each solution to 1 d.p.}$$
Chapter 10 - Trigonometric Identi.hint: $$\text{Write }\sin^2x=1-\cos^2x,\ \text{let }c=\cos x,\ \text{solve the quadratic, then convert back to angles.}$$
Chapter 10 - Trigonometric Identi.correct_answer: $$\begin{aligned}8\sin^2x+6\cos x-9&=0\\8(1-\cos^2x)+6\cos x-9&=0\\8-8\cos^2x+6\cos x-9&=0\\-8\cos^2x+6\cos x-1&=0\\8\cos^2x-6\cos x+1&=0\\\text{Let }c=\cos x:\quad 8c^2-6c+1&=0\\c&=\frac{6\pm\sqrt{36-32}}{16}=\frac{6\pm2}{16}\\c&=\frac12\ \text{or}\ \frac14\\[4pt]\cos x=\frac12&\Rightarrow x=60^\circ,\ 300^\circ\\[2pt]\cos x=\frac14&\Rightarrow x=\cos^{-1}\!\left(\frac14\right),\ 360^\circ-\cos^{-1}\!\left(\frac14\right)\\\cos^{-1}\!\left(\frac14\right)&\approx75.522^\circ\\x&\approx75.522^\circ,\ 284.478^\circ\\[4pt]\therefore\ x&=60.0^\circ,\ 75.5^\circ,\ 284.5^\circ,\ 300.0^\circ\end{aligned}$$

Chapter 10 - Trigonometric Identi.question_text: $$\text{Find all solutions in }0^\circ\le x\le360^\circ\text{ to }\sin^2x+1=\frac{7}{2}\cos^2x,\ \text{giving each solution to 1 d.p.}$$
Chapter 10 - Trigonometric Identi.correct_answer: $$\begin{aligned}\sin^2x+1&=\frac{7}{2}\cos^2x\\(1-\cos^2x)+1&=\frac{7}{2}\cos^2x\\2-\cos^2x&=\frac{7}{2}\cos^2x\\2&=\left(\frac{7}{2}+1\right)\cos^2x=\frac{9}{2}\cos^2x\\\cos^2x&=\frac{4}{9}\\\Rightarrow \cos x&=\pm\frac{2}{3}\\[4pt]\cos x=\frac23:&\ x=\cos^{-1}\!\left(\frac23\right),\ 360^\circ-\cos^{-1}\!\left(\frac23\right)\\\cos^{-1}\!\left(\frac23\right)&\approx48.1897^\circ\\x&\approx48.1897^\circ,\ 311.8103^\circ\\[4pt]\cos x=-\frac23:&\ x=\cos^{-1}\!\left(-\frac23\right),\ 360^\circ-\cos^{-1}\!\left(-\frac23\right)\\\cos^{-1}\!\left(-\frac23\right)&\approx131.8103^\circ\\x&\approx131.8103^\circ,\ 228.1897^\circ\\[4pt]\therefore\ x&\approx48.2^\circ,\ 131.8^\circ,\ 228.2^\circ,\ 311.8^\circ\end{aligned}$$

Chapter 10 - Trigonometric Identi.question_text: $$\text{Show that }2\cos^2x+\cos x-6=0\text{ has no solutions (in degrees).}$$
Chapter 10 - Trigonometric Identi.hint: $$\text{Let }c=\cos x.\ \text{If the quadratic gives }|c|>1,\ \text{then no real }x\text{ exists.}$$
Chapter 10 - Trigonometric Identi.correct_answer: $$\begin{aligned}2\cos^2x+\cos x-6&=0\\\text{Let }c=\cos x:\quad 2c^2+c-6&=0\\c&=\frac{-1\pm\sqrt{1-4(2)(-6)}}{2\cdot2}=\frac{-1\pm\sqrt{49}}{4}\\c&=\frac{-1\pm7}{4}\\c&=\frac{6}{4}=1.5\ \text{ or }\ c=\frac{-8}{4}=-2\\\text{But }\cos x&\in[-1,1]\text{ for all real }x\\1.5\notin[-1,1],\ -2\notin[-1,1]&\Rightarrow \text{both are impossible}\\\therefore\ \text{the equation has no real solutions.}\end{aligned}$$

Chapter 11 - Vectors.correct_answer: In the parallelogram, $\overrightarrow{OA}=2\mathbf{m}$ and $\overrightarrow{OB}=2\mathbf{p}$, so $\vec{OC}=\vec{OA}+\vec{OB}=2\mathbf{m}+2\mathbf{p}$. As $N$ is midpoint of $BC$, $\vec{ON}=\dfrac{\vec{OB}+\vec{OC}}{2}=\dfrac{2\mathbf{p}+(2\mathbf{m}+2\mathbf{p})}{2}=\mathbf{m}+2\mathbf{p}$. Then $\overrightarrow{DQ}=\vec{OQ}-\vec{OD}=(2\mathbf{m}+\mathbf{p})-(\mathbf{m}+\mathbf{p})=\mathbf{m}$.

Chapter 11 - Vectors.question_text: The point $B$ lies on the line with equation $2y=12-3x$. Given that $|OB|=\sqrt{13}$, find possible expressions for $\overrightarrow{OB}$ in the form $p\mathbf{i}+q\mathbf{j}$.
Chapter 11 - Vectors.hint: Use line equation $y=(12-3x)/2$ together with circle equation $x^{2}+y^{2}=13$, then solve the resulting quadratic for $x$ and find corresponding $y$.
Chapter 11 - Vectors.correct_answer: On the line $2y=12-3x$ we have $y=\dfrac{12-3x}{2}$. Because $|OB|=\sqrt{13}$, coordinates $(x,y)$ satisfy $x^{2}+y^{2}=13$. Substitute: $$x^{2}+\left(\dfrac{12-3x}{2}\right)^{2}=13.$$ Then $$x^{2}+\dfrac{(12-3x)^{2}}{4}=13\Rightarrow4x^{2}+(12-3x)^{2}=52\Rightarrow4x^{2}+144-72x+9x^{2}=52,$$ $$13x^{2}-72x+92=0.$$ Solving, $$x=\dfrac{72\pm\sqrt{72^{2}-4\cdot13\cdot92}}{2\cdot13}=\dfrac{72\pm\sqrt{5184-4784}}{26}=\dfrac{72\pm20}{26},$$ so $x=2$ or $x=\dfrac{46}{13}$. For $x=2$, $y=\dfrac{12-3\cdot2}{2}=\dfrac{6}{2}=3$, giving $\overrightarrow{OB}=2\mathbf{i}+3\mathbf{j}$. For $x=\dfrac{46}{13}$, $y=\dfrac{12-3\cdot\frac{46}{13}}{2}=\dfrac{12-\frac{138}{13}}{2}=\dfrac{\frac{156-138}{13}}{2}=\dfrac{\frac{18}{13}}{2}=\dfrac{9}{13}$, giving $\overrightarrow{OB}=\dfrac{46}{13}\mathbf{i}+\dfrac{9}{13}\mathbf{j}$. Thus the possible expressions are $2\mathbf{i}+3\mathbf{j}$ and $\dfrac{46}{13}\mathbf{i}+\dfrac{9}{13}\mathbf{j}$.

Chapter 11 - Vectors.correct_answer: For $\triangle OAB$: $\overrightarrow{OA}=2p,\ \overrightarrow{OB}=2r,\ \overrightarrow{AB}=\overrightarrow{OB}-\overrightarrow{OA}=2r-2p=2(r-p).$ For $\triangle PAQ$: $\overrightarrow{PA}=\overrightarrow{OA}-\overrightarrow{OP}=2p-p=p,\ \overrightarrow{PQ}=r$ (from part a-ii), and $\overrightarrow{AQ}=\overrightarrow{OQ}-\overrightarrow{OA}=(p+r)-2p=r-p.$ Thus the three corresponding sides of $\triangle PAQ$ are $p,r,r-p$, which are each exactly half of the corresponding sides $2p,2r,2(r-p)$ of $\triangle OAB$. Therefore all corresponding side lengths are in the ratio $1:2$ and the included angles are equal, so $\triangle PAQ\sim\triangle OAB.$

Chapter 11 - Vectors.question_text: $OAB$ is a triangle with $\overrightarrow{OA}=a$ and $\overrightarrow{OB}=b$. The point $M$ divides $OA$ in the ratio $2:1$ and $MN$ is parallel to $OB$. Express the vector $\overrightarrow{ON}$ in terms of $a$ and $b$.
Chapter 11 - Vectors.hint: Use the fact that $M$ is on $OA$ and similar triangles $AMN$ and $AOB$ (since $MN\parallel OB$) to find $AN$ as a fraction of $AB$, then obtain $ON=OA+AN$.
Chapter 11 - Vectors.correct_answer: Since $M$ divides $OA$ in the ratio $2:1$, taking $OM:MA=2:1$ gives $OM=\tfrac23 a$ and $AM=\tfrac13 a.$ Because $MN\parallel OB$, $\triangle AMN\sim\triangle AOB$ with scale factor $k=AM/AO=(\tfrac13 a)/a=\tfrac13.$ Hence $AN=k\cdot AB=\tfrac13(b-a).$ Therefore $\overrightarrow{ON}=\overrightarrow{OA}+\overrightarrow{AN}=a+\tfrac13(b-a)=a+\tfrac13 b-\tfrac13 a=\tfrac23 a+\tfrac13 b.$

Chapter 11 - Vectors.question_text: With the same triangle as in 3a, show that $AN:NB=1:2$.
Chapter 11 - Vectors.hint: Use the similarity ratio from part (a) to relate $AN$ and $AB$, then deduce $NB$.
Chapter 11 - Vectors.correct_answer: From the similarity in part (a), $AN=\tfrac13 AB$ so the remaining segment is $NB=AB-AN=AB-\tfrac13 AB=\tfrac23 AB.$ Therefore $AN:NB=\tfrac13 AB:\tfrac23 AB=1:2.$

Chapter 11 - Vectors.question_text: $OABC$ is a square. $M$ is the midpoint of $OA$, and $Q$ divides $BC$ in the ratio $1:3$. $AC$ and $MQ$ meet at $P$. If $\overrightarrow{OA}=a$ and $\overrightarrow{OC}=c$, express $\overrightarrow{OP}$ in terms of $a$ and $c$.
Chapter 11 - Vectors.hint: Express all relevant points in terms of $a$ and $c$, form vector equations for lines $AC$ and $MQ$, then solve for the intersection parameter.
Chapter 11 - Vectors.correct_answer: In the square, $A$ has position $a$, $C$ has $c$ and $B$ has $a+c$. Midpoint $M$ of $OA$ has $\overrightarrow{OM}=\tfrac12a$. Point $Q$ divides $BC$ in the ratio $1:3$ with $BQ:QC=1:3$, so $\overrightarrow{OQ}=\tfrac34\overrightarrow{OB}+\tfrac14\overrightarrow{OC}=\tfrac34(a+c)+\tfrac14c=\tfrac34a+c$. Then $\overrightarrow{MQ}=\overrightarrow{OQ}-\overrightarrow{OM}=(\tfrac34a+c)-\tfrac12a=\tfrac14a+c$. A general point on $AC$ is $a+t(c-a)=(1-t)a+tc$, while a general point on $MQ$ is $\tfrac12a+s(\tfrac14a+c)=(\tfrac12+\tfrac{s}{4})a+sc$. At $P$ these are equal, so $(1-t)a+tc=(\tfrac12+\tfrac{s}{4})a+sc$, giving $1-t=\tfrac12+\tfrac{s}{4}$ and $t=s$. Hence $1-t=\tfrac12+\tfrac{t}{4}\Rightarrow4-4t=2+t\Rightarrow2=5t\Rightarrow t=\tfrac25$. Thus $\overrightarrow{OP}=\overrightarrow{OA}+t(\overrightarrow{OC}-\overrightarrow{OA})=a+\tfrac25(c-a)=\tfrac35a+\tfrac25c$.

Chapter 11 - Vectors.question_text: Show that $P$ divides $AC$ in the ratio $2:3$.
Chapter 11 - Vectors.hint: Use the parameter $t$ found on line $AC$ as the fraction of $AC$ from $A$ to $P$.
Chapter 11 - Vectors.correct_answer: From part (a), the position of $P$ on $AC$ is $a+t(c-a)$ with $t=\tfrac25$. This means $AP=\tfrac25\,AC$ and therefore $PC=AC-AP=\tfrac35\,AC$. Hence $AP:PC=2:3$, so $P$ divides $AC$ in the ratio $2:3$.

Chapter 11 - Vectors.question_text: In triangle $ABC$ the position vectors of $A,B$ and $C$ are $\begin{pmatrix}5\\8\end{pmatrix}$, $\begin{pmatrix}4\\3\end{pmatrix}$ and $\begin{pmatrix}7\\6\end{pmatrix}$ respectively. Find $|\overrightarrow{AB}|$.
Using the same triangle, find $|\overrightarrow{AC}|$.
Using the same triangle, find $|\overrightarrow{BC}|$.
Find the sizes of $\angle BAC$, $\angle ABC$ and $\angle ACB$ to the nearest degree.
Chapter 11 - Vectors.hint: Use the dot-product formula $\cos\theta=\dfrac{\vec{u}\cdot\vec{v}}{|\vec{u}||\vec{v}|}$ for the angle between two vectors from the same vertex.
Chapter 11 - Vectors.correct_answer: At $A$, use $\overrightarrow{AB}=\begin{pmatrix}-1\\-5\end{pmatrix}$ and $\overrightarrow{AC}=\begin{pmatrix}2\\-2\end{pmatrix}$: $\overrightarrow{AB}\cdot\overrightarrow{AC}=(-1)(2)+(-5)(-2)=-2+10=8$, $|\overrightarrow{AB}||\overrightarrow{AC}|=\sqrt{26}\cdot2\sqrt2=4\sqrt{13}$, so $\cos\angle BAC=\dfrac{8}{4\sqrt{13}}=\dfrac{2}{\sqrt{13}}\approx0.555$ giving $\angle BAC\approx56^\circ$. At $B$, use $\overrightarrow{BA}=-\overrightarrow{AB}=\begin{pmatrix}1\\5\end{pmatrix}$ and $\overrightarrow{BC}=\begin{pmatrix}3\\3\end{pmatrix}$: $\overrightarrow{BA}\cdot\overrightarrow{BC}=1\cdot3+5\cdot3=18$, $|\overrightarrow{BA}||\overrightarrow{BC}|=\sqrt{26}\cdot3\sqrt2=6\sqrt{13}$, so $\cos\angle ABC=\dfrac{18}{6\sqrt{13}}=\dfrac{3}{\sqrt{13}}\approx0.832$ giving $\angle ABC\approx34^\circ$. At $C$, use $\overrightarrow{CA}=-\overrightarrow{AC}=\begin{pmatrix}-2\\2\end{pmatrix}$ and $\overrightarrow{CB}=-\overrightarrow{BC}=\begin{pmatrix}-3\\-3\end{pmatrix}$: $\overrightarrow{CA}\cdot\overrightarrow{CB}=(-2)(-3)+2(-3)=6-6=0$, hence $\cos\angle ACB=0$ and $\angle ACB=90^\circ$. So the angles are approximately $56^\circ$, $34^\circ$ and $90^\circ$.

Chapter 11 - Vectors.question_text: $\triangle OPQ$ is a triangle with $2\overrightarrow{PR}=\overrightarrow{RQ}$ and $3\overrightarrow{OR}=\overrightarrow{OS}$. Given $\overrightarrow{OP}=a$ and $\overrightarrow{OQ}=b$, show that $\overrightarrow{OS}=2a+b$.
Chapter 11 - Vectors.hint: Use the section formula for point $R$ on $PQ$, then multiply $\overrightarrow{OR}$ by $3$.
Chapter 11 - Vectors.correct_answer: The condition $2\overrightarrow{PR}=\overrightarrow{RQ}$ gives $PR:RQ=1:2$, so $R$ divides $PQ$ in the ratio $1:2$. Thus $\overrightarrow{OR}=\dfrac{2\overrightarrow{OP}+1\overrightarrow{OQ}}{1+2}=\dfrac{2a+b}{3}$. Since $3\overrightarrow{OR}=\overrightarrow{OS}$, we get $\overrightarrow{OS}=3\cdot\dfrac{2a+b}{3}=2a+b$.

Chapter 11 - Vectors.question_text: Point $T$ is added so that $\overrightarrow{OT}=-b$. Prove that points $T,P,S$ lie on a straight line.
Chapter 11 - Vectors.hint: Show that $\overrightarrow{TP}$ and $\overrightarrow{TS}$ are parallel by expressing them in terms of $a$ and $b$.
Chapter 11 - Vectors.correct_answer: From $\overrightarrow{OP}=a$, $\overrightarrow{OS}=2a+b$ and $\overrightarrow{OT}=-b$, we have $\overrightarrow{TP}=\overrightarrow{OP}-\overrightarrow{OT}=a-(-b)=a+b$ and $\overrightarrow{TS}=\overrightarrow{OS}-\overrightarrow{OT}=(2a+b)-(-b)=2a+2b=2(a+b)$. Since $\overrightarrow{TS}=2\overrightarrow{TP}$, the vectors $\overrightarrow{TP}$ and $\overrightarrow{TS}$ are parallel and share point $T$, so $T,P,S$ lie on a straight line.

Chapter 11 - Vectors.question_text: $OPQR$ is a parallelogram, with $\overrightarrow{OP}=a$ and $\overrightarrow{OR}=b$. $N$ is the midpoint of $PQ$ and $M$ is the midpoint of $QR$. The line $ON$ meets the diagonal $PR$ at $X$. Explain why $\overrightarrow{PX}=-ja+jb$, where $j$ is a constant.
Chapter 11 - Vectors.hint: Parametrise the diagonal $PR$ from $P$ towards $R$ and write $\overrightarrow{PX}$ as a scalar multiple of $\overrightarrow{PR}$.
Chapter 11 - Vectors.correct_answer: On the diagonal $PR$, any point $X$ can be written as $X=P+j\,\overrightarrow{PR}$ for some real constant $j$, so $\overrightarrow{PX}=j\,\overrightarrow{PR}=j(b-a)=-ja+jb$, hence $\overrightarrow{PX}=-ja+jb$ for some constant $j$.

Chapter 11 - Vectors.question_text: Show that $\overrightarrow{PX}=(k-1)a+\tfrac12kb$, where $k$ is a constant, given that $X$ also lies on the line $ON$ from the origin.
Chapter 11 - Vectors.hint: Find $\overrightarrow{ON}$ using the midpoint $N$ of $PQ$, then write $\overrightarrow{OX}=k\,\overrightarrow{ON}$ and subtract $\overrightarrow{OP}$.
Chapter 11 - Vectors.correct_answer: In the parallelogram, $P$ has position $a$ and $Q$ has position $a+b$, so their midpoint $N$ has $\overrightarrow{ON}=\dfrac{\overrightarrow{OP}+\overrightarrow{OQ}}{2}=\dfrac{a+(a+b)}{2}=a+\tfrac12 b$. Any point $X$ on $ON$ has $\overrightarrow{OX}=k(a+\tfrac12 b)$, so $\overrightarrow{PX}=\overrightarrow{OX}-\overrightarrow{OP}=k(a+\tfrac12 b)-a=(k-1)a+\tfrac12kb$.

Chapter 11 - Vectors.question_text: Explain why the constants $j$ and $k$ must satisfy the simultaneous equations $k-1=-j$ and $\tfrac12k=j$.
Chapter 11 - Vectors.hint: Equate the two expressions for $\overrightarrow{PX}$ obtained in parts (a) and (b) and compare coefficients of $a$ and $b$.
Chapter 11 - Vectors.correct_answer: From part (a), $\overrightarrow{PX}=-ja+jb$ and from part (b), $\overrightarrow{PX}=(k-1)a+\tfrac12kb$. Since these are equal vectors, their $a$-components and $b$-components must match: $(k-1)a=-ja$ gives $k-1=-j$, and $\tfrac12kb=jb$ gives $\tfrac12k=j$. Thus $k-1=-j$ and $\tfrac12k=j$.

Chapter 11 - Vectors.question_text: Hence find the values of $j$ and $k$.
Chapter 11 - Vectors.correct_answer: From $\tfrac12k=j$ substitute into $k-1=-j$ to get $k-1=-\tfrac12k$, so $k+\tfrac12k=1$ gives $\tfrac32k=1$ and therefore $k=\dfrac{2}{3}$. Then $j=\tfrac12k=\tfrac12\cdot\dfrac{2}{3}=\dfrac{1}{3}$. So $k=\dfrac23$ and $j=\dfrac13$.

Chapter 11 - Vectors.question_title: Division of diagonal $PR$ into three equal parts
Chapter 11 - Vectors.question_text: Deduce that the lines $ON$ and $OM$ divide the diagonal $PR$ into three equal parts.
Chapter 11 - Vectors.hint: Use $j=\tfrac13$ to locate $X$ on $PR$ and similarly find the parameter for $Y$ where $OM$ meets $PR$, then compare the segments along $PR$.
Chapter 11 - Vectors.correct_answer: From part (a), $\overrightarrow{PX}=j\,\overrightarrow{PR}$ and with $j=\tfrac13$ we have $\overrightarrow{PX}=\tfrac13\overrightarrow{PR}$ so $X$ is one third of the way from $P$ to $R$. For the line $OM$, note that $M$ is the midpoint of $QR$ so $Q$ has position $a+b$ and $R$ has $b$, giving $\overrightarrow{OM}=\dfrac{(a+b)+b}{2}=\tfrac12a+b$. A general point $Y$ on $OM$ has $\overrightarrow{OY}=\lambda(\tfrac12a+b)$, and as a point on $PR$ also $\overrightarrow{OY}=\overrightarrow{OP}+t\,\overrightarrow{PR}=a+t(b-a)$ for some $t$. Equating components: from $b$ we get $\lambda=t$, and from $a$ we get $\tfrac12\lambda=1-t$. Substituting $\lambda=t$ gives $\tfrac12t=1-t$ so $\tfrac32t=1$ and $t=\dfrac{2}{3}$. Thus $\overrightarrow{PY}=t\,\overrightarrow{PR}=\dfrac23\overrightarrow{PR}$ so $Y$ is two thirds of the way from $P$ to $R$. Hence $PX=\tfrac13PR$, $PY=\tfrac23PR$, so $XY=PY-PX=\tfrac23PR-\tfrac13PR=\tfrac13PR$ and $YR=PR-PY=\tfrac13PR$. Therefore $PX=XY=YR$ and the lines $ON$ and $OM$ divide the diagonal $PR$ into three equal parts.

Chapter 11 - Vectors.question_text: Find the speed of a particle moving with velocity $(3\mathbf{i}+4\mathbf{j})\ \text{m s}^{-1}$.
Chapter 11 - Vectors.hint: Speed is the magnitude of the velocity vector: $|\vec v|=\sqrt{x^{2}+y^{2}}$.

Chapter 11 - Vectors.hint: Convert $2$ minutes to $120$ seconds and use $\text{distance}=|\vec v|\times t$.

Find the speed and the distance travelled with velocity $(2\mathbf{i}+5\mathbf{j})\ \text{m s}^{-1}$ for $3$ seconds.

Chapter 11 - Vectors.question_text: A particle $P$ is accelerating at a constant rate. When $t=0$, $P$ has velocity $\mathbf{u}=(2\mathbf{i}+3\mathbf{j})\ \text{m s}^{-1}$ and at time $t=5\ \text{s}$, $P$ has velocity $\mathbf{v}=(16\mathbf{i}-5\mathbf{j})\ \text{m s}^{-1}$. The acceleration vector is given by $\mathbf{a}=\dfrac{\mathbf{v}-\mathbf{u}}{t}$. Find the acceleration of $P$ in terms of $\mathbf{i}$ and $\mathbf{j}$.
Chapter 11 - Vectors.hint: Subtract the initial velocity from the final velocity, then divide by the time interval $5$ s.

Chapter 11 - Vectors.question_text: A particle $P$ of mass $m=0.3\ \text{kg}$ moves under a single constant force $\mathbf{F}$ newtons. The acceleration of $P$ is $\mathbf{a}=(5\mathbf{i}+7\mathbf{j})\ \text{m s}^{-2}$. Find the angle between the acceleration and $\mathbf{i}$.
Chapter 11 - Vectors.hint: UUse $\tan\theta = \dfrac{\text{y-component}}{\text{x-component}} = \dfrac{7}{5}$ for the angle to the positive $x$-axis.

Chapter 11 - Vectors.question_text: With the information in 5a and using $\mathbf{F}=m\mathbf{a}$, find the magnitude of $\mathbf{F}$.

Two forces $\mathbf{F}_1$ and $\mathbf{F}_2$ are given by $\mathbf{F}_1=(3\mathbf{i}-4\mathbf{j})\ \text{N}$ and $\mathbf{F}_2=(p\mathbf{i}+q\mathbf{j})\ \text{N}$. The resultant force $\mathbf{R}=\mathbf{F}_1+\mathbf{F}_2$ acts in a direction parallel to the vector $(2\mathbf{i}-\mathbf{j})$. Find the angle between $\mathbf{R}$ and the vector $\mathbf{i}$.
Chapter 11 - Vectors.hint: Since $\mathbf{R}$ is parallel to $2\mathbf{i}-\mathbf{j}$, use the angle between $2\mathbf{i}-\mathbf{j}$ and $\mathbf{i}$: $\cos\theta=\dfrac{\vec v\cdot\mathbf{i}}{|\vec v||\mathbf{i}|}$.
Chapter 11 - Vectors.correct_answer: Let $\vec v=2\mathbf{i}-\mathbf{j}=(2,-1)$. Then $\vec v\cdot\mathbf{i}=2$, $|\vec v|=\sqrt{2^{2}+(-1)^{2}}=\sqrt{5}$, $|\mathbf{i}|=1$. Hence $\cos\theta=\dfrac{2}{\sqrt5}$ so $\theta=\cos^{-1}\left(\dfrac{2}{\sqrt5}\right)\approx26.6^\circ.$

Chapter 11 - Vectors.question_text: Show that $p+2q=5$.
Chapter 11 - Vectors.correct_answer: $\mathbf{R}=(3+p)\mathbf{i}+(-4+q)\mathbf{j}$ is parallel to $2\mathbf{i}-\mathbf{j}$, so $\mathbf{R}=k(2\mathbf{i}-\mathbf{j})=(2k)\mathbf{i}+(-k)\mathbf{j}$. Thus $3+p=2k$ and $-4+q=-k$, so $k=4-q$. Substituting $k$ into $3+p=2(4-q)$ gives $3+p=8-2q\Rightarrow p+2q=5.$

Chapter 11 - Vectors.question_text: Given that $p=1$, find the magnitude of $\mathbf{R}$.
Chapter 11 - Vectors.hint: First find $q$ from $p+2q=5$, then compute $\mathbf{R}=\mathbf{F}_1+\mathbf{F}_2$ and its magnitude.
Chapter 11 - Vectors.correct_answer: From $p+2q=5$ with $p=1$ we get $1+2q=5\Rightarrow2q=4\Rightarrow q=2$. Then $\mathbf{F}_2=\mathbf{i}+2\mathbf{j}$ and $\mathbf{R}=(3\mathbf{i}-4\mathbf{j})+(\mathbf{i}+2\mathbf{j})=(4\mathbf{i}-2\mathbf{j})$. Hence $|\mathbf{R}|=\sqrt{4^{2}+(-2)^{2}}=\sqrt{16+4}=\sqrt{20}=2\sqrt5\ \text{N}.$

Chapter 11 - Vectors.question_text: The field $ABC$ is a triangle. Given $\overrightarrow{AB}=30\mathbf{i}+40\mathbf{j}$ metres and $\overrightarrow{AC}=40\mathbf{i}-60\mathbf{j}$ metres, find $\overrightarrow{BC}$.
Find the size of $\angle BAC$, in degrees, correct to one decimal place.
Find the area of the field in square metres.
Chapter 11 - Vectors.hint: Use the $2$-D vector cross-product magnitude: $\text{Area}=\dfrac12|\overrightarrow{AB}\times\overrightarrow{AC}|$, where $|\vec u\times\vec v|=|u_xv_y-u_yv_x|$.

Chapter 11 - Vectors.question_text: A boat has position vector $(2\mathbf{i}+\mathbf{j})$ km and a buoy has position vector $(6\mathbf{i}-4\mathbf{j})$ km relative to origin $O$. Find the distance of the boat from the buoy.
Chapter 11 - Vectors.hint: Form the displacement vector from boat to buoy and find its magnitude.

Chapter 11 - Vectors.question_text: Find the bearing of the boat from the buoy.
Chapter 11 - Vectors.hint: Use the vector from buoy to boat $(-4\mathbf{i}+5\mathbf{j})$; find angle from north using $\tan\theta=\dfrac{\text{east}}{\text{north}}$ and convert to a bearing $0^\circ$–$360^\circ$.
Chapter 11 - Vectors.correct_answer: Vector from buoy to boat is $(2\mathbf{i}+\mathbf{j})-(6\mathbf{i}-4\mathbf{j})=(-4\mathbf{i}+5\mathbf{j})$, i.e. $4$ km west and $5$ km north. Let $\theta$ be the angle west of north: $\tan\theta=\dfrac{4}{5}\Rightarrow\theta\approx38.7^\circ.$ Bearings are measured clockwise from north; going towards the northwest gives bearing $360^\circ-\theta\approx360^\circ-38.7^\circ\approx321^\circ.$

Chapter 11 - Vectors.question_text: The boat travels with constant velocity $(8\mathbf{i}-10\mathbf{j})$ km h$^{-1}$. Verify that the boat is travelling directly towards the buoy and find the speed of the boat.
Chapter 11 - Vectors.hint: Compare the direction of the velocity with the displacement from boat to buoy; if they are scalar multiples the motion is directly towards the buoy. Speed is the magnitude of velocity.
Chapter 11 - Vectors.correct_answer: The displacement from boat to buoy is $(4\mathbf{i}-5\mathbf{j})$. The velocity $\mathbf{v}=(8\mathbf{i}-10\mathbf{j})=2(4\mathbf{i}-5\mathbf{j})$ is a positive scalar multiple of this displacement, so the boat travels directly towards the buoy. The speed is $|\mathbf{v}|=\sqrt{8^{2}+(-10)^{2}}=\sqrt{64+100}=\sqrt{164}=2\sqrt{41}\ \text{km h}^{-1}.$

Chapter 11 - Vectors.question_text: Work out how long it will take the boat to reach the buoy.

Two forces $\mathbf{F}_1$ and $\mathbf{F}_2$ act on a particle. $\mathbf{F}_1=-3\mathbf{i}+7\mathbf{j}$ newtons and $\mathbf{F}_2=\mathbf{i}-\mathbf{j}$ newtons. The resultant force $\mathbf{R}$ is given by $\mathbf{R}=\mathbf{F}_1+\mathbf{F}_2$. Calculate the magnitude of $\mathbf{R}$ in newtons.
Chapter 11 - Vectors.hint: Add the two vectors to get $\mathbf{R}$, then find its magnitude $|\mathbf{R}|=\sqrt{x^{2}+y^{2}}$.

Chapter 11 - Vectors.question_text: With $\mathbf{R}=-2\mathbf{i}+6\mathbf{j}$ from part (a), calculate, to the nearest degree, the angle between the line of action of $\mathbf{R}$ and the vector $\mathbf{j}$.
Chapter 11 - Vectors.hint: Use the dot product formula $\cos\theta=\dfrac{\mathbf{R}\cdot\mathbf{j}}{|\mathbf{R}||\mathbf{j}|}$, where $\mathbf{j}=(0,1)$.

Chapter 11 - Vectors.question_text: At $09{:}00$, a small boat $S$ has position vector $(-2\mathbf{i}-4\mathbf{j})$ km relative to a fixed origin $O$ (with $\mathbf{i}$ due east and $\mathbf{j}$ due north). At $09{:}40$, $S$ is at $(4\mathbf{i}-6\mathbf{j})$ km. Calculate the bearing on which $S$ is drifting.
Chapter 11 - Vectors.hint: Find the displacement vector $\overrightarrow{OS_2}-\overrightarrow{OS_1}$, resolve into east and north components, then convert its direction into a three-figure bearing measured clockwise from north.
Chapter 11 - Vectors.correct_answer: Initial position $\overrightarrow{OS_1}=(-2,-4)$, final position $\overrightarrow{OS_2}=(4,-6)$. Displacement $\overrightarrow{S_1S_2}=\overrightarrow{OS_2}-\overrightarrow{OS_1}=(4,-6)-(-2,-4)=(6,-2)$, i.e.\ $6$ km east and $2$ km south. The direction is $E\,\theta\,S$ where $\tan\theta=\dfrac{2}{6}=\dfrac{1}{3}$, so $\theta=\tan^{-1}\!\left(\dfrac{1}{3}\right)\approx18.4^\circ$. Bearing from north is $090^\circ+\theta\approx90^\circ+18.4^\circ=108.4^\circ\approx108^\circ$ (to nearest degree).

Chapter 11 - Vectors.question_text: With the same information, find the speed of $S$.
Chapter 11 - Vectors.hint: Speed $=\dfrac{\text{distance travelled}}{\text{time}}$; use the magnitude of the displacement and time $40$ minutes $=\dfrac{2}{3}$ h.

Chapter 11 - Vectors.question_text: A football is kicked from point $A$ and its motion is modelled as a particle with constant velocity $(4\mathbf{i}+9\mathbf{j})\ \text{m s}^{-1}$. Find the speed of the ball.
Chapter 11 - Vectors.hint: Speed is the magnitude of the velocity vector: $|\vec v|=\sqrt{4^{2}+9^{2}}$.

Chapter 11 - Vectors.question_text: Using the same model, find the distance of the ball from $A$ after $6$ seconds.
Chapter 11 - Vectors.hint: Distance travelled with constant speed is $\text{speed}\times\text{time}$.
Chapter 11 - Vectors.correct_answer: From part (a) the speed is $\sqrt{97}\ \text{m s}^{-1}$. In $6$ s, distance $=\sqrt{97}\times6=6\sqrt{97}\ \text{m}.$

Chapter 11 - Vectors.question_text: Comment on the validity of this constant-velocity model for large values of $t$.
Chapter 11 - Vectors.hint: Consider real motion of a ball under gravity and air resistance compared with a constant-velocity assumption.
Chapter 11 - Vectors.correct_answer: In reality the ball is subject to gravity and air resistance, so its velocity changes: it follows a curved trajectory, slows down, and eventually lands, bounces or stops. The assumption of constant velocity is only reasonable for a very short time immediately after the kick; for large $t$ the model is not valid because it ignores these forces and the ball cannot continue indefinitely in a straight line at constant speed.

Chapter 11 - Vectors.question_text: $ABCD$ is a trapezium with $AB\parallel DC$ and $DC=4AB$. Point $M$ divides $DC$ such that $DM:MC=3:2$. Given $\overrightarrow{AB}=a$ and $\overrightarrow{BC}=b$, find $\overrightarrow{AM}$ in terms of $a$ and $b$.
Chapter 11 - Vectors.hint: Take $A$ as origin, find position vectors of $B,C,D,M$, then subtract to obtain $\overrightarrow{AM}$.
Chapter 11 - Vectors.correct_answer: Let $A$ be the origin. Then $\overrightarrow{AB}=a\Rightarrow B:a$, $\overrightarrow{BC}=b\Rightarrow C:a+b$. Since $DC=4AB$, $\overrightarrow{DC}=4a$ so $C=D+4a\Rightarrow D=(a+b)-4a=-3a+b$. With $DM:MC=3:2$, $\overrightarrow{DM}=\dfrac{3}{5}\overrightarrow{DC}=\dfrac{3}{5}\cdot4a=\dfrac{12}{5}a$, so $M=D+\overrightarrow{DM}=(-3a+b)+\dfrac{12}{5}a=-\dfrac{3}{5}a+b$. Thus $\overrightarrow{AM}=\overrightarrow{OM}=-\dfrac{3}{5}a+b$.

Chapter 11 - Vectors.question_text: In the same trapezium, find $\overrightarrow{BD}$ in terms of $a$ and $b$.
Chapter 11 - Vectors.hint: Use the position vectors $B:a$ and $D=-3a+b$ and subtract.

Chapter 11 - Vectors.question_text: In the same trapezium, find $\overrightarrow{MB}$ in terms of $a$ and $b$.
Chapter 11 - Vectors.hint: Subtract the position vector of $M$ from that of $B$.

Chapter 11 - Vectors.question_text: In the same trapezium, find $\overrightarrow{DA}$ in terms of $a$ and $b$.
The vectors $5a+kb$ and $8a+2b$ are parallel. Find the value of $k$.
Chapter 11 - Vectors.hint: If $5a+kb$ is parallel to $8a+2b$ then $5a+kb=\lambda(8a+2b)$ for some $\lambda$; equate coefficients of $a$ and $b$.
Chapter 11 - Vectors.correct_answer: Assume $5a+kb=\lambda(8a+2b)=8\lambda a+2\lambda b$. Then $5=8\lambda$ and $k=2\lambda$. From $5=8\lambda$ we get $\lambda=\dfrac{5}{8}$, hence $k=2\lambda=2\cdot\dfrac{5}{8}=\dfrac{5}{4}$.

Chapter 11 - Vectors.question_text: Given $a=\begin{pmatrix}7\\4\end{pmatrix}$, $b=\begin{pmatrix}10\\-2\end{pmatrix}$ and $c=\begin{pmatrix}-5\\-3\end{pmatrix}$, find $a+b+c$.
Chapter 11 - Vectors.hint: Add the components of the three vectors.

Chapter 11 - Vectors.correct_answer: Let $\overrightarrow{AB}=(3,5)$ and $\overrightarrow{AC}=(6,3)$. Then $\overrightarrow{AB}\cdot\overrightarrow{AC}=3\cdot6+5\cdot3=18+15=33$. Also $|\overrightarrow{AB}|=\sqrt{3^{2}+5^{2}}=\sqrt{34}$, $|\overrightarrow{AC}|=\sqrt{6^{2}+3^{2}}=\sqrt{45}=3\sqrt{5}$. The resultant of vectors $a=4\mathbf{i}-3\mathbf{j}$ and $b=2p\,\mathbf{i}-p\,\mathbf{j}$ is parallel to $c=2\mathbf{i}-3\mathbf{j}$. Find the value of $p$.
Chapter 11 - Vectors.hint: Set $\mathbf{R}=a+b$ and require $\mathbf{R}=\lambda c$ for some $\lambda$; compare components to solve for $p$.
Chapter 11 - Vectors.correct_answer: $\mathbf{R}=a+b=(4+2p)\mathbf{i}+(-3-p)\mathbf{j}$. If $\mathbf{R}$ is parallel to $c=2\mathbf{i}-3\mathbf{j}$ then $(4+2p,-3-p)=\lambda(2,-3)=(2\lambda,-3\lambda)$. Hence $4+2p=2\lambda$ and $-3-p=-3\lambda$. From the second: $3\lambda=3+p\Rightarrow\lambda=1+\dfrac{p}{3}$. Substitute into the first: $4+2p=2\left(1+\dfrac{p}{3}\right)=2+\dfrac{2p}{3}\Rightarrow2=\dfrac{2p}{3}-2p=-\dfrac{4p}{3}\Rightarrow p=-\dfrac{3}{2}$.

(Equivalently, from the equations we get $\lambda=\dfrac12$ and $\mathbf{R}=\dfrac12(2\mathbf{i}-3\mathbf{j})=\mathbf{i}-\dfrac{3}{2}\mathbf{j}$.)

Chapter 11 - Vectors.correct_answer: $|\mathbf{a}|=\sqrt{p^{2}+q^{2}}=15\Rightarrow p^{2}+q^{2}=225$. Since $\mathbf{a}$ makes angle $55^\circ$ with $\mathbf{i}$, its components are $p=15\cos55^\circ$ and $q=15\sin55^\circ$. Thus $p=15\cos55^\circ,\ q=15\sin55^\circ$ (both positive).

In $\triangle OAB$, $\overrightarrow{OA}=\mathbf{a}$ and $\overrightarrow{OB}=\mathbf{b}$. The point $M$ divides $OA$ in the ratio $3:2$ and $MN$ is parallel to $OB$. Express the vector $\overrightarrow{ON}$ in terms of $\mathbf{a}$ and $\mathbf{b}$.
Chapter 11 - Vectors.hint: Write $\overrightarrow{OM}$ as a fraction of $\mathbf{a}$, then let $\overrightarrow{ON}= \mathbf{a}+t(\mathbf{b}-\mathbf{a})$ (since $N$ lies on $AB$) and use $MN\parallel\mathbf{b}$ to find $t$.
Chapter 11 - Vectors.correct_answer: $OM:MA=3:2\Rightarrow\overrightarrow{OM}=\dfrac{3}{5}\mathbf{a}$. Let $N$ lie on $AB$, so $\overrightarrow{ON}=\mathbf{a}+t(\mathbf{b}-\mathbf{a})=(1-t)\mathbf{a}+t\mathbf{b}$. Then $\overrightarrow{MN}=\overrightarrow{ON}-\overrightarrow{OM}=(1-t)\mathbf{a}+t\mathbf{b}-\dfrac{3}{5}\mathbf{a}=\left(\dfrac{2}{5}-t\right)\mathbf{a}+t\mathbf{b}$. For $\overrightarrow{MN}\parallel\mathbf{b}$, the coefficient of $\mathbf{a}$ must be $0$, so $\dfrac{2}{5}-t=0\Rightarrow t=\dfrac{2}{5}$. Hence $\overrightarrow{ON}=(1-\dfrac{2}{5})\mathbf{a}+\dfrac{2}{5}\mathbf{b}=\dfrac{3}{5}\mathbf{a}+\dfrac{2}{5}\mathbf{b}$.

Chapter 11 - Vectors.correct_answer: The direction vector is $\mathbf{v}=3\mathbf{i}-\mathbf{j}$. Then $\mathbf{v}\cdot\mathbf{i}=3$, $|\mathbf{v}|=\sqrt{3^{2}+(-1)^{2}}=\sqrt{10}$. Chapter 11 - Vectors.question_text: With the same information, show that $p+3q=11$.
Chapter 11 - Vectors.hint: Let $\mathbf{R}=(4+p)\mathbf{i}+(-5+q)\mathbf{j}$ and set $\mathbf{R}=\lambda(3\mathbf{i}-\mathbf{j})$; compare coefficients of $\mathbf{i}$ and $\mathbf{j}$.
Chapter 11 - Vectors.correct_answer: $\mathbf{R}=\mathbf{F}_1+\mathbf{F}_2=(4+p)\mathbf{i}+(-5+q)\mathbf{j}$. Since $\mathbf{R}=\lambda(3\mathbf{i}-\mathbf{j})=(3\lambda)\mathbf{i}+(-\lambda)\mathbf{j}$, we have $4+p=3\lambda$ and $-5+q=-\lambda\Rightarrow\lambda=5-q$. Substituting gives $4+p=3(5-q)=15-3q\Rightarrow p+3q=11$.

Chapter 11 - Vectors.question_text: The point $B$ lies on the line with equation $3y=12-5x$. Given that $\lvert OB\rvert=\dfrac{3\sqrt{10}}{2}$, find two possible expressions for $\overrightarrow{OB}$ in the form $p\mathbf{i}+q\mathbf{j}$.
Chapter 11 - Vectors.hint: Let $B=(x,y)$ satisfy both the line $3y=12-5x$ and the circle $x^{2}+y^{2}=\left(\dfrac{3\sqrt{10}}{2}\right)^{2}$; solve the simultaneous equations, then write the two corresponding vectors.
Chapter 11 - Vectors.correct_answer: Let $B=(x,y)$ with $3y=12-5x\Rightarrow y=\dfrac{12-5x}{3}$. The magnitude condition gives $x^{2}+y^{2}=x^{2}+\left(\dfrac{12-5x}{3}\right)^{2}=\left(\dfrac{3\sqrt{10}}{2}\right)^{2}=\dfrac{45}{2}$. Thus $x^{2}+\dfrac{(12-5x)^{2}}{9}=\dfrac{45}{2}$. Multiply by $18$: $18x^{2}+2(12-5x)^{2}=405\Rightarrow18x^{2}+2(144-120x+25x^{2})=405\Rightarrow68x^{2}-240x-117=0$. Solving gives $x=\dfrac{240\pm36\sqrt{69}}{136}=\dfrac{60\pm9\sqrt{69}}{34}$. Then $y=\dfrac{12-5x}{3}=\dfrac{36\mp15\sqrt{69}}{34}$. Hence the two possible position vectors are $\overrightarrow{OB}=\dfrac{60+9\sqrt{69}}{34}\,\mathbf{i}+\dfrac{36-15\sqrt{69}}{34}\,\mathbf{j}$ and $\overrightarrow{OB}=\dfrac{60-9\sqrt{69}}{34}\,\mathbf{i}+\dfrac{36+15\sqrt{69}}{34}\,\mathbf{j}$.
